title.en: Two Feathers and Turkey Brother: The Impostor in the Hollow Tree
title.zh: 雙羽與火雞弟：空心樹裡的冒名者

region.en: Trail to the great chief's village beyond the river, Seneca country
region.zh: 塞內卡之地大河彼岸大酋長村落的獵徑

source.archive: Internet Archive (Buffalo Historical Society Publications, vol. 27)
source.work: A. C. Parker, Seneca Myths and Folk Tales, ch. VI tale 21, 'Two Feathers and Turkey Brother' (1923)

summary.en: Two Feathers receives his dream-protectors - a great spider and a great black snake - and from his uncle's treasure chest the panther-skin costume whose heron feathers watch, whose fisher-skin bag bites, whose pipe-bear growls, and whose medicine root lets him spit wampum. Warned of three enchanted spots, he nonetheless helps a boy at the oak (the sorcerer's wife is knocked into her own fire), drains three monsters from the poisoned spring and burns them - screech-owls fly from their bursting heads - and then, despite every warning, shoots the old man's raccoon, strips off his magic clothes and climbs after it into the hollow tree. The treacherous uncle shoves him down among the bones, dons the magic costume, woos the chief's daughter across the river and marries her. Two Feathers is rescued by spider and snake, appears at the lodge looking like a sick old man in dirty clothes, eats the marriage bread, regains his wampum root when the impostor's bag bites him, and outdoes him bowl for bowl - dark wampum for lizards and toads, white wampum for round worms. When the gluttonous impostor finally sleeps, Two Feathers kills a great herd of deer, dons his magic suit which brightens as it touches him, and grows young; the council sees the costume's powers, the false husband is kicked into the garbage hole, and all the people follow the hero home.
summary.zh: 雙羽得夢中護靈——大蜘蛛與大黑蛇；又自叔父的百寶箱得到豹皮神裝：鴺羽守望、魚貂袋噬敵、熊頭菸斗低吼、藥根吐貝珠。雖被警告三處魔地，他仍助樹下男孩（巫婆被推入自焚）、放盡毒泉的三頭怪物焚之（怪首爆裂飛出啼鴞），卻不聽勸阻射了老翁的浣熊、脫下神衣攀樹入洞。老巫把他推落枯骨之間，披上神裝渡河娶走大酋長之女。蜘蛛與黑蛇救出雙羽；他以襤褸老翁之貌赴宴成婚，趁冒名者被魚貂咬傷之際拾回藥根，一碗吐出烏貝珠勝其蜥蟾蛆蟲，再一碗白貝珠勝其圓蟲。饕餮的冒名者爛醉睡死，雙羽獵鹿成群、披上神衣煥然一新、重返青春。議會上神裝顯靈，假婿被踢入垃圾洞，全族隨英雄凱旋。

sensitivity.note: Seneca tale (Parker 1923); public domain. The spitting-wampum motif is Parker's signature of Seneca magic.

passages.text: On the tenth day of his fast Two Feathers saw a great spider dropping down from the tops of the trees, and it spoke to him saying, 'When you are in great distress I will be your protector.' Again he saw a great black snake rising from the ground and when it had reached the tops of the trees it spoke saying, 'When you are in great distress and need a strong friend, I will be your protector.' His uncle then opened his treasure chest and gave him, after rejecting two costumes, a panther-skin shirt with the head of the panther as a cap and two heron feathers above it. 'The heron feathers on your hood will watch out for you and when you are in danger they will speak. Your fisher skin bag is alive and should anyone seek to harm you when asleep it will bite him... The medicine will give you power to spit wampum. The black end of the root will make dark wampum and the white end will make white wampum. Your pipe has the head of a bear upon it and it will growl when an enemy touches it, while the snakes on the bowl will hiss when you light your tobacco.'
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 173-175; not verbatim.

passages.text: 'As you journey from here you will find three enchanted spots, and all must be avoided... a certain tree where there will be a boy playing about. He will ask you to lift him from the ground... do not touch the boy for a sorcerer lives in the tree... a deep spring where there is sparkling water... there are monsters living in it who will draw you in and drown you... a grove of very tall trees. Here you will see an old man who will hop around strangely. He will ask you to shoot a raccoon... He will be the cause of your ruin if you heed his pleas.' They traveled very rapidly, until by noon they had traveled a distance that takes ordinary people three years to go. At the oak Two Feathers placed the boy on a stump under the tree, and as he did this there was a great roar and two gigantic arms came down and grabbed the stump, fixing it to the tip of a large arrow; the stump flew through the air into the witch's lodge and knocked her into the fire.
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 175-177; not verbatim.

passages.text: At the bubbling spring Three monsters leaped from the water and were dragged out and burned, their heads bursting with shrieks as a flock of screech-owls flew away - the clearing had been a prosperous village whose people the sorcerers had poisoned by dragging them into the depths of the water. At the tall trees the old man cried, 'Oh my nephews, there is a raccoon on that branch and I have no bow or arrow.' Two Feathers would not listen to Turkey, who flew about gobbling, and shot the raccoon - which ran down a large hole at the top of the tree. 'Oh my nephew, climb after it for me. Take it off beneath the tree and I will watch it for you.' Up he went like a squirrel, but as he stood looking down into the hole the old man shoved him in, down into a pit beneath the roots where he smelt the flesh of victims and felt their bones beneath his feet.
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 177-178; not verbatim.

passages.text: The old man went to the clothing Two Feathers had left behind: 'Now I shall be able to cross the river and take the great man's daughter as my wife.' Renewed in body and more handsome with every step, he wooed the elder sister, ate the wedding bread and was married. Two Feathers called his friend Spider, who let down a strand of web that broke and dropped him, then his friend Black Snake, who coiled about him and drew him forth. In the dirty clothing left by the old man he looked like a sick old man, and the girl ferried him across, declaring, 'I am the only girl whom you can marry.' At supper the impostor reached into his bag and cried out, for the fisher bit his wrist; in dropping the bag the magic medicine fell out, and Two Feathers grabbed it and hid it in his bosom. In the morning he filled a bark bowl with dark wampum to the brim, while the impostor's emetic produced lizards, toads and worms; a second bowl of white wampum beat round worms. At last the gluttonous impostor slept, and Two Feathers dragged a great quantity of deer to the lodge and put on his own fine clothing - immediately it became bright and new, and he grew young again. His wife kicked the impostor out of bed, made him put on his old clothes and thrust him into the garbage hole, and nobody ever saw him again.
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 179-183; not verbatim.

title.en: Two Feathers and Woodchuck Leggings: The Death Charm and the White Eagle
title.zh: 雙羽與土撥鼠綁腿：死亡咒物與白鵰

region.en: Do'ciowe' and the Valley of the Pleasant River (Ganundaseg), Seneca country
region.zh: 塞內卡之地的多喬維與樂河之谷

source.archive: Internet Archive (Buffalo Historical Society Publications, vol. 27)
source.work: A. C. Parker, Seneca Myths and Folk Tales, ch. VI tale 22, 'Two Feathers and Woodchuck Leggings' (1923)

summary.en: Two Feathers, kind to the animals he can talk to, receives the powerful arrow of an old man in a bark house, and wins the love of Drooping Flower: 'something went out of his eyes into her eyes, and something went out of her eyes into his.' When famine strikes the valley village he sings a magic song and shoots four arrows into the air - 'Bring me meat from different animals' - and a deer, a moose, an elk and a bear run singing to the lodge and drop dead at his feet; he blows a stream of wampum beads over a tanned skin and the starving village feasts. The jealous uncle Woodchuck Leggings allies with the girl's witch mother, whose dream-demands he must satisfy: the antlers of the two great elk of the cold lake (shot in darkness, the arrow flashing light to reveal them), the shell-coated pelts of the wampum deer, two white beavers of the hot lake - and each gift only increases her rage. Then, camped by the fire, Woodchuck Leggings plunges the death charm of hickory bark between Two Feathers' shoulders, dons his white clothes and fails every test of the costume - his birds bashful, his pouch limp, his breath breathing out loathly worms - and marries instead the pitying sister Wiaso'. The forest animals Two Feathers has befriended nourish him with their blood; a year later the crippled 'Old-Bones-with-a-cough' wins the tournament by bringing down the great white eagle with a single spoken arrow, the stranger who suggests they ask him is his friend the wolf, the arrow clings to his finger, and in the sweat lodge of fat bear skins he pulls the charm from his neck and kills Woodchuck Leggings with it. His ruined suit restores as it touches him; the witch mother, revealed, chews off her own fingers and vanishes down the dog-tracks to a pond with neither inlet nor outlet.
summary.zh: 雙羽善待能與之對話的百獸，得老翁所贈的神箭，贏得「垂花」的愛：『他眼中有光渡入她眼中，她眼中的光也渡入他眼中。』河谷村鬧饑荒時，他唱咒歌、朝天連射四箭——「把不同野獸的肉帶給我」——鹿、駝鹿、麋與熊唱著歌奔至門前倒斃；他朝獸皮吐出貝珠雨，全村得以飽餐。妒忌的叔父土撥鼠綁腿勾結巫婆岳母，其夢索屢屢加碼：寒湖雙巨麋之角（黑暗中箭光閃亮照出）、貝殼鹿之皮、熱湖白河狸——禮物愈貴重，巫婆愈怒。營火之側，土撥鼠綁腿把山核桃皮死亡咒物刺入雙羽肩胛，穿上白衣，卻樣樣失靈——鳥兒害羞、袋子癱軟、吐出的是蠕蟲——轉而娶了憐惜他的姐姐。雙羽受他善待過的群獸以血哺之；一年後，跛咳的「老骨咳」以一支言出法隨的神箭射落白鵰奪魁——提議「去問咳嗽老人」的陌生人正是他救過的狼。箭應指而懸，熊脂汗屋中他拔出頸後咒物，反手擊斃土撥鼠綁腿。破舊的神衣觸體復新；巫婆原形畢露，自噬其指，化犬遁入無出無入的池塘。

sensitivity.note: Seneca tale (Jimerson informant 1903, Parker 1923); public domain. Parker's note: Edward Cornplanter criticized the version's Christian-informant details but approved it for white readers.

passages.text: Two Feathers was a hunter and never feared to hunt any animal, but he was kind to the animals and could talk to them, so they became his friends. He had a pet bear in a small yard and he had a wolf that he had tamed. He said that it was the same as a man... He had fine clothes. They were made of white buckskin and embroidered all over with porcupine quills. He had also a tobacco pouch made of a spotted fawn's skin with the feet and head on and in this he kept a pipe having a bear's head carved on it, and eyes that rolled when the jaws of the bear chewed the tobacco inside. He had a gustoh'we' (feathered hat), with two feathers in front, and on the hat there were two chirping birds. Two Feathers acquired magic and became very strong, but he did not let anyone know that he was Hotci'non'ga', a charm holder. 'I have been looking for you a long time,' said the old man in the bark house. 'You have been merciful to me and I am going to give you my arrow. It does not look like a good arrow, but most truly it has great power.'
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 184-185; not verbatim.

passages.text: He noticed two girls, one older and one younger, named Drooping Flower. He looked at the younger girl and she looked at him, and something went out of his eyes into her eyes, and something went out of her eyes into his. He said to himself, 'That's the one.' One of the villagers saw this and told Two Feathers that he was now under the spell of a very evil witch, the mother of the girl... A runner came to the village and told them that all the people in the valley across the river were starving: hunters had been unable to secure game and the corn harvest had failed. Two Feathers asked all the women who could to gather about their doorways and play the plum-stone game and to sing: 'Ganio daweeni, the game is coming.' He then went into the woods at the edge of the clearing and sang a magic song, taking out four arrows which had lain close to the arrow the old man had given him. One by one he shot the arrows into the air, each in a different direction, at the same time calling, 'Bring me meat from different animals.'... there was a song in the air: 'The wild animals are coming.' Four animals came running to the doorway where Two Feathers sat waiting. Each animal had an arrow sticking in its heart: a deer, a moose, an elk and a bear.
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 185-186; not verbatim.

passages.text: The starving village then had food and Drooping Flower recovered... He began to make a noise like 'tsiit, tsut, tsit.' Opening his mouth wide he blew out a great stream of wampum beads. Immediately there was a scramble for the beads and nearly everybody grabbed a handful. As Two Feathers left the house he saw the jealous, blazing eyes of his uncle, Woodchuck Leggings... That night Two Feathers and Woodchuck Leggings slept on one side of the witch's lodge. Midnight came and the old woman began to have a bad dream... 'I have had a dream and must be satisfied. Oh I must have the antlers of two large buck elk that live in a cold lake. I must have them by morning or direful things will happen.'... Long he swam into the darkness, for there was no starlight or moon. Taking his arrow from an oiled skin bag he spoke to it and then shot. There was a great flash of light in the sky and the mysterious lake elk were revealed. The arrow had pierced both of them... 'I am sorry I had to kill you, but the woman desired it in satisfaction of a dream.' The elks spoke again, 'The woman has deceived you.' The gift of the great antlers only increased the old woman's anger: next the pelts of the wampum-coated deer, then two white beavers of the hot lake - 'You may have the meat, but I will keep the skins' - and each gift only made her more angry.
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 187-190; not verbatim.

passages.text: The crafty old scoundrel watched his opportunity. When Two Feathers was fast asleep, he made his way stealthily to the other side of the fire and drew from his shirt a long sharp point of hickory bark. It was the death charm. Kneeling at his back he lifted the bark high above his head and brought it down with all his strength, plunging it into the back of his victim just between the shoulders. Removing his own dirty garments, Woodchuck Leggings replaced them with the beautiful white clothes of Two Feathers... 'Here comes Two Feathers!'... 'You are not real Two Feathers,' she exclaimed. 'Where is Two Feathers?' 'I am he!' 'Sonohweh! You are a liar!'... he called the council, but his birds were bashful and his commands were in vain; the foul fumes filled the lodge and nearly stifled the people; the pouch clung to his side limper than ever; from his mouth flew a quantity of small white cylinders - clusters of loathly worms... Two Feathers awoke after several days' unconsciousness and found a great herd of forest animals about him. 'Our brother, you have been sick,' said the wolf, the spokesman. 'You were stabbed by Woodchuck Leggings as you were sleeping. But as you were kind, so we are not ungrateful and our blood has kept you nourished while you slept.'... 'Old-Bones-with-a-cough' touched the arrow, it clung to his finger and followed his hand into the air... With a loud cry Two Feathers pulled the bark point from his neck and before the cringing man before him had time to utter a sound, Two Feathers struck him a heavy blow over the neck. The death charm sank into the flesh, passed between the bones in his back and Woodchuck Leggings lay dead... Only tracks of a big dog could be seen leading from the lodge. They were traced to a pond which had neither inlet nor outlet, and there they stopped. It was found out she had been a witch.
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 190-199; not verbatim.
